title: Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act of 2018
official_summary:
Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act of 2018

This bill requires the Department of State to report to Congress annually regarding the level of access Chinese authorities granted U.S. diplomats, journalists, and tourists to Tibetan areas in China. Such assessment shall include:

  • a comparison with the level of access granted to other areas of China,
  • a comparison between the levels of access granted to Tibetan and non-Tibetan areas in relevant provinces,
  • a comparison of the level of access in the reporting year and the previous year, and
  • a description of the measures that impede the freedom to travel in Tibetan areas.

No individual who is substantially involved in the formulation or execution of policies related to access for foreigners to Tibetan areas may enter the United States if:

  • the requirement that foreigners must receive official permission to enter the Tibet Autonomous Region remains in effect, or has been replaced by a similar regulation that also requires foreigners to gain a level of permission to enter the Tibet Autonomous Region that is not required for other provinces; and
  • travel restrictions on U.S. diplomats, officials, journalists, and citizens to Tibet Autonomous areas in Sichuan, Qinghai, Yunnan, and Gansu Provinces are greater than travel restrictions to other areas.

The State Department shall report to Congress annually, identifying individuals who were blocked from U.S. entry during the preceding year and a list of Chinese officials who were substantially involved in the formulation or execution of policies to restrict the access of U.S. diplomats, journalists, and citizens to Tibetan areas.

summary.headline: This law requires yearly State Department reports on U.S. access to Tibetan areas of China and allows entry bans on certain Chinese officials tied to those access limits.
summary.what_it_does: The State Department must report to Congress each year on how much access Chinese authorities give U.S. diplomats, journalists, and tourists to Tibetan areas, comparing it with other parts of China and with the prior year. The report must also describe measures that limit travel in Tibetan areas. The law lets the U.S. refuse entry to officials substantially involved in restricting foreign access to the Tibet Autonomous Region, if the permit rule stays in place or is replaced by a similar rule that treats foreigners more strictly than other provinces, and travel limits in Tibetan areas of Sichuan, Qinghai, Yunnan, and Gansu are greater than elsewhere. The State Department must also name blocked individuals and list the Chinese officials involved each year.

who_it_affects.group: Chinese officials involved in setting or carrying out policies that limit foreign access to Tibetan areas
who_it_affects.how: They may be barred from entering the United States if the access conditions in the law are met, and they are named in annual State Department reports.

who_it_affects.group: U.S. diplomats, journalists, and citizens who travel to Tibetan areas of China
who_it_affects.how: The State Department must track and report on the travel limits they face, though the law does not directly change their own travel rules.

who_it_affects.group: Foreign tourists seeking to visit the Tibet Autonomous Region
who_it_affects.how: The annual reports compare their access to that of other parts of China, but the law does not itself change permit requirements.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: Enacted December 19, 2018; the annual reporting and entry-ban provisions apply from that date, with reports due each year afterward.
